messages.subject: Plotted Smooths DSM question
parts:
Hello All,

I was wondering if there were a way to normalize the y-axis for the plots of smooth terms from the DSM in R. I know the y-axis is currently on the link-scale from the GAM, but is there code to convert this back to the response scale and still keep the confidence band around the smooth?

Any help or suggestions would be appreciated. This is not a necessity, but just an interest.

Thanks,

John

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Plotted Smooths DSM question
parts:
John

My reading of the documentation for "plot.gam" which produces the plots in question, implies to me that it can only plot on the scale of the linear predictor.  The alternative is to perform the coding yourself using predict.gam() with the arguments type="response" and se.fit=TRUE

That will cough out a 2-element list; first element being the point estimates on the response scale and standard errors in the second element (note documentation states "(possibly with approximate standard errors).").  You'll then build the plots of interest yourself.

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Plotted Smooths DSM question
parts:
Hi John, hi listfolk,

Indeed, Eric is correct and this is possible using the plot.gam command
(in fact you can use the trans= argument to transform the values).

BUT I'd argue that this is not the right thing to do. By transforming
the plots to the response scale you start to think about looking up
values on the plot to see what the abundance effect would be -- this
doesn't quite make sense as each plot shows the effect of only one
smooth (with everything else set to zero). If you did the transformation
to the exponential (response) scale, you need to also include the offset
to be able to make the y axis make sense in this situation. In that
case, you need to add that to all of the plots to get a "prediction" for
a single point, but by adding the offset to each plot you destroy the
additive nature of the plots (as you'll add the offset multiple times).

I think it's safer to avoid this interpretation of the plots, and leave
things on the link scale.


Caveat: This kind of plot can be useful in a couple of situations:

1. when there is only 1 smooth, then the plot has a logical interpretation.
2. when the other smooths in the model (the ones that are not plotted)
can be held at a given value -- e.g., if you have a "treatment" effect
(e.g., raise in sea surface temperature of 3C) that you want to show the
effect of. In that case you still need to hold everything else constant.


I realise it's tempting to make these plots, especially when presenting
results, as it seems like it's an easy way for folks to "see" the
results. However, interpretation is tricky and in some sense the
capacity for over/misinterpretation is higher when converting to the
abundance scale. In a perverse way, it might be "safer" to stick with a
plot that no one understand and can't misinterpret than one that folks
can easily misinterpret.


Hope this helps,
--dave

Thanks to Eric and Dave,

I appreciate your assistance and your advice. I understand the potential issues when dealing with multiple smooths within a model. However, I am currently just looking at the effects of individual covariates to determine their effects on density, thus running a model with only a single covariate smooth. Given their is only one covariate, is it still advisable to restrain from normalizing the plots. I can get basic trends in relationships between the 2 without normalizing, but since we are specifically looking at the effects of single covariates I had thought getting the y-axis to the response scale would provide more relevant information.

Best,

John

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Plotted Smooths DSM question
parts:
Hi John, hi listfolk,

Yes, with a single smooth, you're in my point 1., below and you're fine.
I'm not sure how much information one can get from such models as given
the highly (non-linearly) correlated the covariates usually are in such
an analysis, you're likely to find some spurious results. For example,
looking at elevation may lead you to think that your study species is
interested in (say) higher areas but in fact once you include a
vegetation, you see that all the variation is taken up by that (because
the species in question really enjoys alpine trees, say).

I don't mean to trash your approach and certainly as an initial
exploratory pass through the data when you're not sure what covariates
are relevant, it's not a bad idea. But fitting models with many
covariates in and looking at the resulting smooths might give you a
better idea of what's going on.

In some sense the single covariate smooth approach will tell you what
you don't need, but it won't tell you what you definitely do.

Hope this helps.

cheers,
--dave
